newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav economy plunges into recession-institute.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav economy plunges into recession-institute.

text.p: Yugoslavia's economy has plunged into a deep recession which should dictate a radical change in government policy the Belgrade-based Institute for Market Research (IZIT) said on Friday.
"The picture of our economy is sad and ugly and the business climate is the worst for six months," IZIT director Jovan Todorovic told reporters.
"It is ugly because of increasing insolvencies, low utilisation of capacity, growing unemployment, a burgeoning trade gap and a decline in living standards."

Todorovic said Yugoslavia needed urgently to rejoin international financial institutions but also to embark on privatisation, restructuring of the economy and a reform of the expensive state apparatus.
The West has made any return to bodies such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) conditional on political as well as economic change by the socialist government.

Three months of political turmoil over local election fraud last November has brought the country closer to the abyss with a deterioration of the economy and mounting social tensions, IZIT's latest report said.

After strong monetary expansion in December and a plunge in the dinar black market rate, the central bank restored financial discipline and sopped up surplus liquidity by cutting the M1 money supply down to 5.5 billion dinars ($1 billion).
The January monetary contraction, despite stabilising the dinar and calming monthly inflation to 1.4 percent from over four percent in December, also produced a fresh blow to the economy's liquidity.
According to central bank's Accounting and Payments Office, there were 21,927 insolvent companies and banks at the end of January, six percent less than in December.
But their unpaid liabilities grew by 29 percent, hitting 6.513 billion dinars and exceeding the M1 money supply by 25 percent, said IZIT economist Tomislav Milisavljevic.

A strong contraction in the money supply further depressed economic activity, with overall industry output plunging 20.8 percent against its December level and construction industries performance falling by around 10 percent.
"The plunge cannot be attributed to seasonal problems, but to a three-month fall in industry orders," Milisavljevic added.

Around 300 companies polled by IZIT cited liquidity problems, lack of commercial credits, high input prices, low capacity utilisation, surplus labour, low purchasing power and a huge fiscal burden as major difficulies.
While economists cast doubt on growth potential, businesses hoped for some economic revival and believed idle capacity and the pool of unemployed labour justified moderate optimism.
The IZIT survey showed 62 per cent of Yugoslav companies would seek direct foreign investment or a form of co-operation or co-production with foreigners.
Eight percent said they would attract capital through capitalisation issues while some of them would opt for a total sell-off to foreigners.
But analysts said attempts to attract foreign investment were wishful thinking in a stalled economy performing in choatic conditions, with the government protecting debtors instead of creditors.
"Growing indebtedness is tolerated by the government which is only trying to buy social peace. And the biggest debtors are big state companies," said an analyst who declined to be named.
The analyst cited the Power Industry of Serbia (EPS), Jugopetrol, NIS Naftagas as the biggest loss-makers.
"As long as the state protects them and does not tackle the problem in a market-oriented way, this economy will be blocked by insolvencies." -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
